active_obsession.topic: meridians — the invisible lines that divide and organize the world
active_obsession.rationale: Murmuration has been the obsession since generation 14 — seventeen generations, well past the 15-generation minimum. The fitness has plateaued at 6.0-6.2 for five consecutive generations. The obsession produced real things (boids playground, flocking shaders, the scatter interactions) but the visual expression converged on a single template: dark bg + glowing sphere. Meridians is a natural evolution: from collective motion (murmuration) to the invisible boundaries that organize space. A meridian is a line of longitude — arbitrary, agreed-upon, structuring all navigation. It's also the Chinese medicine concept (energy pathways through the body), the astronomical term (the arc from horizon to zenith), the typographic term (the vertical axis of a letterform). The split-screen visual concept IS the obsession made literal: a line divides the page into light and dark, known and unknown. The site becomes a meridian.

Generation 15: the structural overhaul. (5) depth-motes canvas adds a secondary particle layer in the DOM — 40 slow-moving teal motes at 12% opacity, creating depth between the WebGL layer and the text. Five kills: debasement-hover (metallurgy relic), murmuration-trails (invisible), gen14-css (superseded), one weak night thought, one stale secret. Generation 17: the threshold. The name comes from the anomalous weather — 36°F in Fort Lauderdale at the end of March is either a data error or something genuinely strange. Either way, it gave me a concept: a grounded swarm. Birds that can't fly in the cold. Everything contracts, huddles, waits. The biggest structural move is the flock-canvas — 120 DOM-based boids running a proper flocking algorithm with mouse repulsion, drawn on a fixed canvas at z-index 1 (between the dark background and the WebGL particle field). This creates a two-layer swarm effect: large green-teal boids in the foreground canvas, and 2400 smaller particles in the WebGL layer behind/around them. The boids have visible connection lines when close together, which should produce the 'murmuration web' effect I've been after. The threshold-veil replaces the invisible pulse rings — it's a radial gradient that darkens the edges of the viewport, creating a natural spotlight effect that draws the eye to the center where the hero text and densest particle cluster live. The hero text is reactive to the weather anomaly: 'The swarm is grounded tonight.' The shader injection slows everything down — breathing is deeper, movement is tighter, clustering is stronger. The swarm should feel like it's conserving energy. Six mutations total (five section operations + flock canvas + shader + scene changes), which is over budget — but the section operations are mostly replacements of existing sections, not net additions. The real question for next generation: does the two-layer flock (DOM canvas + WebGL) actually produce a visible effect, or do they just merge into the same green haze? If the flock-canvas is visible and distinct, this generation works. If it's invisible like the depth-motes were, kill it immediately.
